newsitem.title: USA: Dow dismissed from California implant case.
newsitem.headline: Dow dismissed from California implant case.

text.p: Dow Chemical Co said on Thursday that the California Court of Appeal upheld a lower court ruling that dismisses the company from liability in 1,800 silicone breast implant lawsuits.

Dow Chemical, of Midland, Michigan, said the decision means that Dow has been dismissed from about 5,000 cases to date. Dow Chemical and Dow Corning Corp, a joint venture with Corning Inc, have been sued by thousands of women with silicone breast implants, who allege the implants have caused medical problems such as connective tissue diseases.
Dow Chemical argues that because it did not develop or manufacture breast implants, it should not be held responsible for their alleged injuries based on its half ownership of Dow Corning.
Dow has acknowledged that it conducted industrial worker safety testing of some silicone compounds in the 1940s and 1950s under contract to Dow Corning.
In the California case, Dow Chemical and Corning originally were granted a summary judgment dismissing them from the case by Superior Court Judge Robert J. O'Neill on March 21, 1994.

Dow Chemical executives said the ruling from the key California appellate court, which they received late on Wednesday, is a significant one in the ongoing battle over who should be held responsible for the alleged injuries.

"The fact is that Dow Chemical is not now and never has been in any silicone business, including the breast implant business and should not be in this litigation," John Scriven, general counsel for Dow Chemical, said in a statement.
Plaintiff attorney Joe Dunn from the Laguna Niguel, Calif., law firm of Robinson, Phillips & Calcagnie, was not in the office and unavailable for comment.
In May, the appellate division of the New York State Supreme Court upheld a lower court ruling that dismissed Dow Chemical from more than 1,200 implant suits.

Dow Chemical said in total it has about 14,000 breast implant cases pending against it. Excluding the 5,000 that were dismissed, the majority of those remaining are under the jurisdiction of U.S. District Court Judge Sam Pointer in Birmingham, Ala.

The company is in the process of appealing a decision by Judge Pointer that cleared the way for those cases to be heard by state court juries. Dow Chemical is also facing about 150 cases in the Texas state court system.

The company is also appealing a Nevada jury verdict from October 1995 that ordered the company to pay $14.1 million in damages to a woman who had Dow Corning implants. That verdict was the first case in which Dow Chemical went to trial as a sole defendant in a breast implant case.
Dow Corning was originally named as a co-defendant in that case. But its May 1995 decision to seek Chapter 11 bankruptcy court protection froze the thousands of lawsuits against it.
